newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Contested U.N. health chief to step down in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Contested U.N. health chief to step down in 1998.

text.p: Hiroshi Nakajima, chief of the World Health Organisation and a frequent target for Western criticism, said on Wednesday he would step down next year when his current mandate runs out.

Nakajima, a 69-year-old pharmacologist, made the announcement -- confirmed by a WHO spokesman -- to Japanese reporters as he prepared for next week's 50th anniversary session of the WHO's annual Assembly.
"I feel two terms as Director-General is adequate and I will not be standing for a third term," Japanese journalists quoted him as saying.
An account of his remarks issued by the WHO said he felt three terms at the head of the organisation was too long "and during the third term various problems could arise."
Nakajima also believed that "he could best continue promoting WHO reform if he were not involved in an election campaign," according to the official account.

The United States, long one of the fiercest critics of his management, greeted the announcement with a diplomatically- worded statement from Health Secretary Donna Shalala who hailed "the important contributions" he had made to the WHO.
She said the 193 members of the WHO should now choose a director-general who could help the body "lead and succeed" in the 21st century.

Former Norwegian prime minister Gro Harland Brundtland, a medical doctor by training, said earlier this month she would like the job. Another candidate is Pakistani woman doctor Nafis Sadik of the U.N. Population Fund.

Nakajima, whose public image was often clouded by his less than perfect command of English and French, was the first Japanese to be given the top job in a United Nations agency when he was appointed in 1988.
The Tokyo government at the time campaigned strongly on his behalf. But more recently Japanese officials have been discreetly distancing themselves from him, diplomats say.

In his first term, he quickly came under fire for what Western countries said was his inadequate control of expenditure and a staff policy which they argued put unqualified people who supported him in key posts.

As the end of his first five-year mandate loomed in early 1993, support from developing countries helped him survive a bid by the United States and European states to replace him with one of his deputies, a respected Algerian doctor.

But two years later in 1995 he was bitterly attacked by several African countries for "racial slander" in remarks at a closed meeting they saw as suggesting people from the continent were not up to holding top jobs.

Zimbabwe's Health Minister Terence Stamps told the WHO Assembly in May that year that Nakajima did not appear to understand "that leadership is about setting a vision and motivating people....and not about command and control."

But the Africans pulled back at the last moment from pushing for his departure, and at the same Assembly he also survived the resignation of the WHO's external auditor who complained of lack of Cooperation from senior officials.
The auditor, also Britain's Auditor-General Sir John co-operation had issued a report two years earlier criticising the WHO's contracting procedures and travel arrangements under Nakajima.
